title: Human rights (Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario)

items.title: Human Rights Code
items.says: Ontario's Human Rights Code sets out the right to equal treatment without discrimination in five social areas. No one may infringe these rights, directly or indirectly.

source.expect: No person shall infringe or do, directly or indirectly

items.title: The Code overrides other laws
items.says: If another Ontario law requires or allows conduct that breaks Part I of the Code, the Code applies and wins, unless that other law says specifically that it applies despite the Code.

source.expect: this Act applies and prevails unless the Act or regulation

items.title: The Code binds the Ontario government
items.says: The Code applies to the Ontario government and its agencies, as well as to private persons and businesses.

source.expect: This Act binds the Crown and every agency of the Crown

items.title: Statutory Powers Procedure Act applies at the HRTO
items.says: The Statutory Powers Procedure Act sets general hearing rules for the Tribunal. Where it conflicts with the Code, its regulations or the Tribunal's rules, those win.

source.expect: apply to a proceeding before the Tribunal unless they conflict

items.title: HRTO Rules of Procedure
items.says: The Tribunal makes its own rules of practice and procedure. The rules must give parties a chance to make oral submissions before an application within its jurisdiction is finally decided, and a final decision must have written reasons.

source.expect: may make rules governing the practice and procedure before it

items.title: Flexible procedure
items.says: The Tribunal's part of the Code and its rules are read broadly, so the Tribunal can use alternatives to traditional courtroom procedures that lead to fair, just and quick resolution of the merits.

source.expect: shall be liberally construed to permit the Tribunal

items.title: What the Tribunal can decide
items.says: The Tribunal can decide every question of fact or law that comes up in an application before it.

source.expect: to determine all questions of fact or law that arise

items.title: How the Tribunal deals with applications
items.says: The Tribunal uses the procedures in its rules, or other procedures available to it, that it thinks give the best chance of a fair, just and quick resolution of the merits.

source.expect: best opportunity for a fair, just and expeditious resolution

items.title: Judicial Review Procedure Act
items.says: The Judicial Review Procedure Act is the law that lets a party ask the Divisional Court to review a Tribunal decision.

source.citation: Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
source.expect: application for judicial review

items.title: Canadian Human Rights Act (federal matters)
items.says: Discrimination by federally regulated organizations (for example banks, airlines, telephone companies, the federal government) falls under the Canadian Human Rights Act, not the Ontario Code. Complaints go to the Canadian Human Rights Commission.

source.citation: Canadian Human Rights Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6
source.expect: may file with the Commission a complaint

items.title: Labour arbitrators can apply the Code
items.says: In a unionized workplace, a grievance arbitrator has the power to interpret and apply human rights laws, even if they conflict with the collective agreement.

source.citation: Labour Relations Act, 1995, S.O. 1995, c. 1, Sched. A
source.expect: interpret and apply human rights and other employment-related statutes

items.title: Check: a protected ground in a protected social area
items.says: The Code covers treatment because of a listed ground (such as race, disability, sex, age, creed, family status) in one of five social areas: services, goods and facilities; housing; contracts; employment; and vocational associations. A matter outside these areas is not covered by the Code.

source.expect: equal treatment with respect to services, goods and facilities

items.title: Check: Ontario or federal law?
items.says: The Ontario Code covers provincially regulated employers, landlords and service providers. Federally regulated organizations are covered by the Canadian Human Rights Act instead.

source.citation: Canadian Human Rights Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6
source.expect: the purpose of this Act

items.title: Federal complaint: one-year time limit
items.says: The Canadian Human Rights Commission may decline to deal with a complaint filed more than one year after the last act complained of, or a longer period it allows.

source.citation: Canadian Human Rights Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6
source.expect: more than one year

items.title: Unionized workers: grievance and HRTO
items.says: A unionized worker can raise a human rights issue through a grievance. The Tribunal can put its own application on hold while the grievance goes ahead, and can dismiss it if the grievance has properly dealt with the substance.

source.expect: The Tribunal may defer an application in accordance with

items.title: Free help: Human Rights Legal Support Centre
items.says: The Human Rights Legal Support Centre gives advice and assistance on Code rights, and legal services for making applications, Tribunal proceedings, judicial review, stated cases and enforcing Tribunal orders. It sets its own priorities based on its resources.

source.expect: Advice and assistance, legal and otherwise

items.title: The Human Rights Legal Support Centre
items.says: The Code creates the Human Rights Legal Support Centre, an independent non-profit corporation funded by Ontario.

source.expect: Human Rights Legal Support Centre in English

items.title: The Centre sets its own priorities
items.says: The Centre's objects include setting policies and priorities for its services based on its financial resources, so it does not take on every matter.

source.expect: establish policies and priorities for the provision of support

items.title: Choose: HRTO application or a court action
items.says: A person can apply to the Tribunal, or, if they are suing in court for another legal wrong (such as wrongful dismissal), ask the court for Code remedies in that lawsuit. They cannot do both for the same right at the same time.

source.expect: may not make an application under subsection (1)

items.title: When an HRTO application is barred
items.says: A person cannot apply to the Tribunal about a right if they have a court case asking for Code remedies about the same alleged infringement that is not finished or withdrawn, or if a court has finally decided whether the right was infringed, or the matter has been settled.

source.expect: a court has finally determined the issue of whether the right

items.title: When a court case is 'finally determined'
items.says: A court case is not finally determined while an appeal is still possible and the time to appeal has not run out.

source.expect: a right of appeal exists and the time for appealing has not expired

items.title: One year to apply to the HRTO
items.says: An application must be made within one year after the incident. If there was a series of incidents, the year runs from the last incident in the series.

source.expect: within one year after the last incident in the series

items.title: Applying after the one-year deadline
items.says: The Tribunal can accept a late application if it is satisfied the delay was in good faith and no one affected will suffer substantial prejudice because of the delay.

source.expect: the delay was incurred in good faith and no substantial prejudice

items.title: Services, goods and facilities
items.says: Everyone has the right to equal treatment in services, goods and facilities (such as stores, restaurants, schools, hospitals, police and government services) without discrimination because of race, ancestry, place of origin, colour, ethnic origin, citizenship, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, age, marital status, family status or disability.

source.expect: Every person has a right to equal treatment with respect to services

items.title: Taxes and fees imposed by law are not 'services'
items.says: Under the Code, 'services' does not include a levy, fee, tax or periodic payment imposed by law.

source.expect: does not include a levy, fee, tax or periodic payment imposed by law

items.title: Housing (occupancy of accommodation)
items.says: Everyone has the right to equal treatment in renting or living in housing without discrimination because of the listed grounds, which in housing also include receiving public assistance.

source.expect: with respect to the occupancy of accommodation

items.title: Harassment in housing
items.says: A person living in housing has the right to be free from harassment because of a listed ground by the landlord, the landlord's agent, or another occupant of the same building.

source.expect: harassment by the landlord or agent of the landlord

items.title: 16- and 17-year-olds renting on their own
items.says: A 16- or 17-year-old who has withdrawn from parental control has the right to equal treatment in renting housing without discrimination because they are under 18. Their rental contract can be enforced against them as if they were 18.

source.expect: withdrawn from parental control has a right to equal treatment

items.title: Contracts
items.says: Every person who has legal capacity has the right to contract on equal terms without discrimination because of a listed ground.

source.expect: has a right to contract on equal terms

items.title: Employment
items.says: Every person has the right to equal treatment in employment without discrimination because of a listed ground. In employment, the grounds include 'record of offences'. This covers hiring, pay, conditions, discipline and firing.

source.expect: equal treatment with respect to employment without discrimination

items.title: Harassment at work
items.says: An employee has the right to be free from harassment at work because of a listed ground by the employer, the employer's agent, or another employee.

source.expect: freedom from harassment in the workplace by the employer

items.title: Unions and professional or trade associations
items.says: Every person has the right to equal treatment in membership in a trade union, trade or occupational association, or self-governing profession, without discrimination because of a listed ground.

source.expect: membership in any trade union, trade or occupational association

items.title: Sexual harassment in housing
items.says: A person living in housing has the right to be free from harassment because of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression by the landlord, the landlord's agent, or another occupant of the building.

source.expect: harassment because of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or gender

items.title: Sexual harassment at work
items.says: An employee has the right to be free from harassment at work because of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression by the employer, the employer's agent, or another employee.

source.expect: harassment in the workplace because of sex

items.title: Unwanted sexual advances by someone with power
items.says: Everyone has the right to be free from a sexual solicitation or advance by a person who can give or deny them a benefit or advancement, where that person knows or ought reasonably to know it is unwelcome; and from reprisal or threats for rejecting it.

source.expect: a sexual solicitation or advance made by a person in a position

items.title: Protection from reprisal
items.says: Everyone has the right to claim and enforce their Code rights, to start and take part in Code proceedings, and to refuse to infringe someone else's rights, without reprisal or threat of reprisal.

source.expect: without reprisal or threat of reprisal for so doing

items.title: Discrimination because of who you associate with
items.says: A Code right is infringed where the discrimination is because of a person's relationship, association or dealings with someone identified by a protected ground.

source.expect: relationship, association or dealings with a person or persons

items.title: Discriminatory signs and notices
items.says: A Code right is infringed by publicly displaying a notice, sign, symbol or emblem that shows an intention to infringe Part I rights or to incite infringement. This does not interfere with freedom of expression of opinion.

source.expect: any notice, sign, symbol, emblem, or other similar representation

items.title: Discriminatory job ads
items.says: The employment right is infringed by a job ad or invitation to apply that directly or indirectly classifies or indicates qualifications by a protected ground.

source.expect: an invitation to apply for employment or an advertisement

items.title: Discriminatory application forms and questions
items.says: The employment right is infringed where an application form or a written or oral question to a job applicant directly or indirectly classifies or indicates qualifications by a protected ground.

source.expect: a form of application for employment is used

items.title: Interview questions where the Code permits
items.says: An employer may ask about a protected ground at a personal job interview where discrimination on that ground is allowed by the Code (for example, a genuine job requirement).

source.expect: the asking of questions at a personal employment interview

items.title: Employment agencies
items.says: An employment agency infringes the employment right if it discriminates because of a protected ground in handling applications or referring applicants to employers.

source.expect: an employment agency discriminates against a person

items.title: Benefit and pension plans
items.says: The employment right is infringed where a job is denied or made conditional on joining a benefit, pension or group insurance plan that makes a distinction on a protected ground, subject to the exceptions in the Code.

source.expect: requires enrolment in an employee benefit, pension or superannuation plan

items.title: Compensation when excluded from a plan for disability
items.says: An employer must pay an employee excluded from a benefit, pension or group insurance plan because of disability an amount equal to what the employer would contribute for an employee without a disability.

source.expect: compensation equivalent to the contribution that the employer would make

items.title: Government contracts and grants
items.says: Every Ontario government contract, subcontract, grant or loan is deemed to include a condition that employment rights under the Code will not be infringed in carrying it out.

source.expect: no right under section 5 will be infringed

items.title: What 'disability' means
items.says: Disability is defined broadly: any degree of physical disability caused by injury, birth defect or illness; mental impairment or developmental disability; learning disability; mental disorder; or an injury or disability for which WSIB benefits were claimed or received.

source.expect: a condition of mental impairment or a developmental disability

items.title: Past and perceived disability
items.says: Protection for disability includes a person who has had a disability, or who is believed to have or have had one.

source.expect: is believed to have or to have had a disability

items.title: Pregnancy is covered under 'sex'
items.says: The right to equal treatment without discrimination because of sex includes discrimination because a woman is or may become pregnant.

source.expect: a woman is or may become pregnant

items.title: What 'harassment' means
items.says: Harassment means a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known, or ought reasonably to be known, to be unwelcome.

source.expect: a course of vexatious comment or conduct

items.title: What 'age' means
items.says: Under the Code, 'age' means 18 years or older. People under 18 are protected on other grounds, and 16- and 17-year-olds have a special housing right.

source.expect: means an age that is 18 years or more

items.title: What 'family status' means
items.says: Family status means the status of being in a parent and child relationship.

source.expect: the status of being in a parent and child relationship

items.title: What 'marital status' means
items.says: Marital status means being married, single, widowed, divorced or separated, and includes living with someone in a conjugal relationship outside marriage.

source.expect: the status of being married, single, widowed, divorced or separated

items.title: What 'record of offences' means
items.says: Record of offences (an employment ground only) means a conviction for an offence for which a pardon (record suspension) was granted and not revoked, or a conviction for a provincial offence.

source.expect: an offence in respect of any provincial enactment

items.title: What an applicant must show (prima facie discrimination)
items.says: The applicant must show: (1) they have a characteristic protected by the Code; (2) they experienced an adverse impact in a social area; and (3) the protected characteristic was a factor in the adverse impact. The burden then shifts to the respondent to justify the conduct under the Code's exemptions.

source.decision: Moore v. British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61
source.expect: the protected characteristic was a factor in the adverse impact

items.title: Intent is not required
items.says: Discrimination can be found even where there was no intent to discriminate; the focus is on the effect of the conduct on the person.

source.decision: Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd., [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536

items.title: Standard of proof
items.says: Each element must be proved on a balance of probabilities. The protected ground need only be one factor, not the only factor.

source.decision: Quebec (Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse) v. Bombardier Inc., 2015 SCC 39

items.title: Constructive (adverse effect) discrimination
items.says: A Code right is infringed where a requirement, qualification or factor that is not itself a protected ground excludes, restricts or prefers a group identified by a protected ground that the person belongs to, unless it is reasonable and bona fide in the circumstances, or the Code (other than s. 17) says that discriminating on that ground is not an infringement.

source.expect: results in the exclusion, restriction or preference of a group

items.title: Constructive discrimination: accommodation required first
items.says: A requirement is not 'reasonable and bona fide' unless the Tribunal or court is satisfied the group's needs cannot be accommodated without undue hardship, considering cost, outside sources of funding, and health and safety requirements. Standards prescribed by regulation must be considered.

source.expect: cannot be accommodated without undue hardship on the person responsible

items.title: Respondent's justification
items.says: Once discrimination is shown on its face, the respondent may justify it only within the Code's exemptions and defences, such as a bona fide requirement where accommodation to the point of undue hardship is not possible, special programs, or the listed exceptions.

source.decision: Moore v. British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61
source.expect: within the framework of the exemptions available under human rights statutes

items.title: Duty to accommodate disability
items.says: A person is not found unable to perform the essential duties of a right (such as a job) because of disability unless the needs of the person cannot be accommodated without undue hardship on the person responsible, considering cost, outside sources of funding, and health and safety requirements.

source.expect: the needs of the person cannot be accommodated without undue hardship

items.title: Essential duties
items.says: A right is not infringed only because a person cannot perform the essential duties or requirements of the right because of disability, but only after accommodation to the point of undue hardship has been considered.

source.expect: incapable of performing or fulfilling the essential duties

items.title: Undue hardship: three factors
items.says: Undue hardship is measured by three things the Code lists: cost, outside sources of funding (if any), and health and safety requirements (if any). A tribunal or court must also consider any standards set by regulation.

source.expect: shall consider any standards prescribed by the regulations

items.title: Accommodation has a procedural and a substantive part
items.says: The duty to accommodate includes a fair process of seeking out and assessing accommodation (gathering information, considering options) and the accommodation itself. The person seeking accommodation is expected to cooperate, and a union may share the duty.

source.decision: Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970

items.title: What must be shown for harassment
items.says: For Code harassment, the applicant shows a course of comment or conduct, connected to a protected ground, in housing or at work, that the harasser knew or ought reasonably to have known was unwelcome. Harassment under ss. 2(2), 5(2) and 7 is not automatically attributed to a corporation under s. 46.3.

source.expect: known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome

items.title: What must be shown for reprisal
items.says: For reprisal, the applicant shows they claimed or enforced Code rights, took part in a Code proceeding, or refused to infringe someone's rights, and that the respondent took or threatened action against them for doing so.

source.expect: to institute and participate in proceedings under this Act

items.title: When a company is responsible for its employees' acts
items.says: An act by an officer, employee or agent of a corporation, union, association or employers' organization in the course of employment is deemed to be the act of that organization, except for harassment under ss. 2(2), 5(2) and 7 and offences. The Tribunal must say, if asked, whether the act was done with the organization's authority or acquiescence.

source.expect: shall be deemed to be an act or thing done or omitted

items.title: Opinion on authority or acquiescence
items.says: At the organization's request, the Tribunal states in its decision whether the employee's act was done with or without the organization's authority or acquiescence.

source.expect: with or without the authority or acquiescence

items.title: Bona fide occupational requirement (employment)
items.says: Discrimination in employment because of age, sex, record of offences or marital status is not an infringement if it is a reasonable and bona fide qualification because of the nature of the job. It is not reasonable and bona fide unless the person's circumstances cannot be accommodated without undue hardship.

source.expect: is a reasonable and bona fide qualification because of the nature of the employment

items.title: A job requirement needs accommodation to the point of undue hardship
items.says: No tribunal or court may find a qualification reasonable and bona fide unless the person's circumstances cannot be accommodated without undue hardship, considering cost, outside funding and health and safety.

source.expect: the circumstances of the person cannot be accommodated without undue hardship

items.title: Organizations serving a particular group
items.says: A religious, philanthropic, educational, fraternal or social organization mainly serving a group identified by certain grounds may hire only, or prefer, people of that group if the qualification is reasonable and bona fide because of the nature of the job.

source.expect: employs only, or gives preference in employment to, persons similarly identified

items.title: Personal or medical care in the home
items.says: An individual may refuse to employ someone for any ground where the main duty of the job is attending to the medical or personal needs of that individual or of an ill child or an aged, infirm or ill spouse or relative.

source.expect: attending to the medical or personal needs of the person

items.title: Hiring or preferring family members
items.says: An employer may grant or withhold employment or advancement to a spouse, child or parent of the employer or an employee.

source.expect: the spouse, child or parent of the employer or an employee

items.title: Special programs
items.says: A Code right is not infringed by a special program designed to relieve hardship or economic disadvantage, or to help disadvantaged persons or groups achieve equal opportunity. The Tribunal can find that a program qualifies even if the Commission has not designated it.

source.expect: a special program designed to relieve hardship or economic disadvantage

items.title: Asking the Commission to designate a special program
items.says: A person may apply to the Ontario Human Rights Commission to designate a program as a special program. A designation lasts up to five years and can be renewed. It does not apply to programs run by the Ontario government.

source.expect: may apply to the Commission for a designation of a program

items.title: Preferences for people 65 and over
items.says: The age right is not infringed where being 65 or over is a requirement for preferential treatment (such as seniors' discounts).

source.expect: an age of sixty-five years or over is a requirement

items.title: Canadian citizenship required by law
items.says: The citizenship right is not infringed where Canadian citizenship is a requirement imposed or authorized by law, and in some cultural, educational, union, athletic and senior executive settings.

source.expect: Canadian citizenship is a requirement, qualification or consideration imposed

items.title: Organizations serving a particular group (services)
items.says: Rights to equal treatment in services and facilities are not infringed where membership in a religious, philanthropic, educational, fraternal or social organization mainly serving a group identified by a protected ground is limited to that group.

source.expect: primarily engaged in serving the interests of persons identified by a prohibited ground

items.title: Religious officials and marriage
items.says: A registered religious official may refuse to solemnize a marriage, or allow a sacred place to be used for one, if it would be contrary to their religious beliefs or their religious body's doctrines.

source.expect: refuses to solemnize a marriage

items.title: Separate school rights
items.says: The Code does not adversely affect separate school rights under the Constitution Act, 1867 and the Education Act.

source.expect: any right or privilege respecting separate schools

items.title: Single-sex facilities for public decency
items.says: The services right is not infringed because of sex where use of services or facilities is restricted to people of the same sex on the ground of public decency.

source.expect: restricted to persons of the same sex on the ground of public decency

items.title: Minimum drinking age
items.says: The age-based services right is not infringed by Ontario's minimum drinking age of 19.

source.expect: enforcing a minimum drinking age of nineteen years

items.title: Recreational clubs
items.says: A recreational club may restrict access or give fee preferences because of age, sex, marital status or family status.

source.expect: where a recreational club restricts or qualifies access

items.title: Sharing a kitchen or bathroom with the owner
items.says: The housing right is not infringed where the housing is in a home where the owner or owner's family lives and the occupant must share a bathroom or kitchen with them.

source.expect: required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner

items.title: Single-sex residential buildings
items.says: The housing right is not infringed because of sex where all units in the building (other than the owner's) are restricted to people of the same sex.

source.expect: is restricted to persons who are of the same sex

items.title: Permitted tenant screening
items.says: A landlord may use income information, credit checks, credit references, rental history, guarantees or similar practices in choosing tenants, but only in the way the regulation prescribes.

source.expect: income information, credit checks, credit references, rental history

items.title: Regulation on landlords' screening practices
items.says: The regulation under the Code sets out how landlords may use income information, credit checks, credit references, rental history and guarantees in selecting tenants.

source.citation: O. Reg. 290/98 (Business Practices Permissible to Landlords in Selecting Prospective Tenants for Residential Accommodation)
source.expect: income information

items.title: Insurance contracts
items.says: Automobile, life, accident, sickness or disability insurance, group insurance (not through an employer) and life annuities may make distinctions based on age, sex, marital status, family status or disability on reasonable and bona fide grounds.

source.expect: on reasonable and bona fide grounds because of age, sex, marital status

items.title: Plans that comply with the Employment Standards Act
items.says: The employment right is not infringed because of age by a benefit, pension or group insurance plan that complies with the Employment Standards Act, 2000 and its regulations.

source.expect: that complies with the Employment Standards Act, 2000

items.title: Pre-existing disability in insurance plans
items.says: A disability or life insurance plan may make a reasonable and bona fide distinction because of a pre-existing disability that substantially increases the risk.

source.expect: a pre-existing disability that substantially increases the risk

items.title: Filing an application with the HRTO
items.says: A person who believes their Code rights were infringed may apply to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario for an order, within one year of the incident or the last incident in a series. The application must be on the Tribunal's approved form.

source.expect: the person may apply to the Tribunal for an order under section 45.2

items.title: Application form (Form 1)
items.says: An application must be made in the form approved by the Tribunal (Form 1, the Application under section 34). The form asks for the social area, the grounds, the facts, and the remedy sought.

source.expect: shall be in a form approved by the Tribunal

items.title: Joint applications
items.says: Two or more people who each have a right to apply may file together, subject to the Tribunal's power to separate them.

source.expect: may file the applications jointly

items.title: Applying on behalf of someone else
items.says: A person or organization (other than the Commission) may apply on behalf of another person who could have applied and who consents. The consent must be on the form the Tribunal rules specify, and the same one-year limit applies.

source.expect: may apply on behalf of another person to the Tribunal

items.title: Same time limit for applications on behalf of another
items.says: An application made on someone else's behalf must be made within the same one-year time limit, and the late-filing rule also applies.

source.expect: shall be made within the time period required

items.title: Withdrawing an application made on your behalf
items.says: The person on whose behalf an application was made may withdraw it under the Tribunal's rules.

source.expect: may be withdrawn by the person on behalf of whom the application is made

items.title: Application by the Ontario Human Rights Commission
items.says: The Commission may apply to the Tribunal if it believes it is in the public interest and an order could provide an appropriate remedy. This does not affect an individual's own right to apply; the two are usually heard together.

source.expect: it is in the public interest to make an application

items.title: Ontario Human Rights Commission
items.says: The Commission promotes and protects human rights, approves policies, conducts inquiries, designates special programs, and may apply to or intervene at the Tribunal. It does not take individual complaints.

source.expect: to make applications to the Tribunal under section 35

items.title: Who the parties are

source.expect: Any person against whom an order is sought in the application

items.title: Adding a party

items.title: Commission intervention
items.says: The Commission may intervene in an individual's application on terms the Tribunal sets, and may intervene as a party if the applicant consents.

source.expect: The Commission may intervene in an application under section 34

items.title: Tribunal checks the application

source.expect: may decide not to process the documents

items.title: Notice of intent to dismiss (jurisdiction or requirements)
items.says: Before dismissing a proceeding without a hearing because it is frivolous, vexatious, in bad faith, outside the Tribunal's jurisdiction, or missing a statutory requirement, the Tribunal must give notice and consider written submissions made within the time stated.

source.expect: the proceeding relates to matters that are outside the jurisdiction

items.title: Written submissions on a proposed dismissal
items.says: A party who receives a notice of intent to dismiss may make written submissions within the time set in the notice, and the Tribunal must consider them before dismissing.

source.expect: may make written submissions to the tribunal with respect to the dismissal

items.title: Respondent files a Response

items.title: Response form (Form 2)

source.expect: Response

items.title: If the respondent does not respond

source.citation: Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario Rules of Procedure (amended effective August 17, 2026)
source.expect: deemed to have accepted

items.title: Applicant's Reply
items.says: An applicant may file a Reply to answer new matters raised in the Response, within the time set by the HRTO Rules.

source.citation: Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario Rules of Procedure (amended effective August 17, 2026)
source.expect: Reply

items.title: Request to defer (put on hold)
items.says: The Tribunal may defer an application, as its rules allow, for example while another proceeding (a grievance, a court action, another tribunal) dealing with the same facts goes ahead.

source.expect: The Tribunal may defer an application

items.title: Request to dismiss because another proceeding dealt with it

source.expect: another proceeding has appropriately dealt with the substance

items.title: Summary hearing request
items.says: A party may ask for, or the Tribunal may hold on its own, a summary hearing on whether all or part of an application should be dismissed because there is no reasonable prospect it will succeed.

source.citation: Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario Rules of Procedure (amended effective August 17, 2026)
source.expect: no reasonable prospect that the Application

items.title: Request for an order during the proceeding
items.says: A party can ask the Tribunal for orders during a proceeding (for example, disclosure, adding a party, adjournment, or anonymizing a decision) using the Tribunal's request form and serving the other parties.

source.citation: Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario Rules of Procedure (amended effective August 17, 2026)
source.expect: Request for Order

items.title: Interim (temporary) order
items.says: The Tribunal can make interim decisions and orders, with conditions, before the final decision. Reasons are not required for an interim order.

source.expect: A tribunal may make interim decisions and orders

items.title: Order for disclosure of documents
items.says: The Tribunal's rules can require a party or other person to produce documents or information, give statements, or produce witnesses in their control. If a party does not comply with such an order, the Tribunal may draw an adverse inference.

source.expect: may draw an adverse inference from the failure of a party

items.title: Request for a Tribunal inquiry
items.says: A party may ask the Tribunal to appoint a person to conduct an inquiry to obtain evidence, if an inquiry is required for evidence, the evidence may help a fair, just and quick resolution, and it is appropriate. The inquirer may enter places (not homes without consent), request documents and question people.

source.expect: an inquiry is required in order to obtain evidence

items.title: Combining or hearing similar cases together
items.says: If two or more proceedings involve similar questions of fact, law or policy, the Tribunal may combine them or hear them together (with consent), hear them back to back, or stay one until another is decided.

source.expect: involve the same or similar questions of fact, law or policy

items.title: Adjournment
items.says: A hearing may be adjourned by the Tribunal on its own or where a party shows an adjournment is needed for an adequate hearing.

source.expect: the adjournment is required to permit an adequate hearing

items.title: Summons to a witness
items.says: The Tribunal can summon any person, including a party, to give evidence or produce documents at a hearing. The summons must be served personally, and a Superior Court judge may issue a warrant if a summoned witness does not attend.

source.expect: A tribunal may require any person, including a party, by summons

items.title: Request to close the hearing or protect privacy
items.says: Hearings are open to the public unless the Tribunal finds public security, or intimate financial or personal matters, outweigh the principle of openness.

source.expect: intimate financial or personal matters or other matters

items.title: Costs at a tribunal
items.says: A tribunal can order costs only if a party acted unreasonably, frivolously, vexatiously or in bad faith and the tribunal has made rules on costs.

source.expect: the conduct or course of conduct of a party has been unreasonable

items.title: Preventing abuse of process
items.says: The Tribunal can make orders or directions to prevent abuse of its processes and can reasonably limit repetitive examination of witnesses.

source.expect: as it considers proper to prevent abuse of its processes

items.title: Mediation
items.says: The Tribunal offers mediation, with the parties' consent, to try to settle the application. A mediator cannot be made to testify about what they learned, and mediation notes are not admissible in a civil proceeding.

source.expect: all parties consent to participating in the alternative dispute resolution

items.title: Mediation is confidential
items.says: A Tribunal mediator cannot be compelled to give testimony or produce documents about matters learned in mediation.

source.expect: shall be compelled to give testimony or produce documents

items.title: Case assessment direction
items.says: If the application does not settle, the Tribunal may issue a case assessment direction setting out the issues, the evidence it needs, and how the hearing will proceed (in person, by video or in writing).

source.citation: Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario Rules of Procedure (amended effective August 17, 2026)
source.expect: case assessment direction

items.title: Exchanging documents and witness lists before the hearing
items.says: Before the hearing, each party must deliver the documents it will rely on and a list of witnesses, with a summary of their expected evidence, by the deadline in the HRTO Rules or the Tribunal's direction.

source.citation: Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario Rules of Procedure (amended effective August 17, 2026)
source.expect: witness statements

items.title: Notice of hearing
items.says: Parties must be given reasonable notice of the hearing, including its time, place and purpose, and a warning that the Tribunal may proceed without them if they do not attend.

source.expect: shall be given reasonable notice of the hearing by the tribunal

items.title: If a party does not attend
items.says: If a party was properly notified and does not attend an oral hearing, the Tribunal may proceed without them, and they are not entitled to further notice.

source.expect: the tribunal may proceed in the absence of the party

items.title: The hearing
items.says: The Tribunal can hold the hearing in person, electronically (video or phone), in writing, or a mix. A party can object to a written hearing for good reason, or to an electronic hearing that would cause significant prejudice.

source.expect: any combination of written, electronic and oral hearings

items.title: Right to make oral submissions
items.says: An application within the Tribunal's jurisdiction cannot be finally decided without giving the parties an opportunity to make oral submissions under the rules.

source.expect: an opportunity to make oral submissions in accordance with the rules

items.title: Representation
items.says: A party may be represented by a representative (a lawyer, a licensed paralegal, or another person the law permits).

source.expect: may be represented by a representative

items.title: Evidence at the hearing
items.says: The Tribunal may admit any relevant oral testimony, document or thing, even if it would not be admissible in court, but not privileged material. It may exclude anything unduly repetitious.

source.expect: relevant to the subject-matter of the proceeding and may act on such evidence

items.title: Calling and cross-examining witnesses
items.says: At an oral or electronic hearing, a party may call witnesses, present evidence and submissions, and cross-examine as reasonably required. The Tribunal's rules can also let it question witnesses and narrow the issues.

source.expect: conduct cross-examinations of witnesses at the hearing

items.title: The Tribunal can narrow issues and limit evidence
items.says: The Tribunal's rules can let it define or narrow the issues, limit evidence and submissions, decide the order of evidence, and conduct examinations of witnesses itself.

source.expect: define or narrow the issues required to dispose of an application

items.title: Ontario Human Rights Commission policies
items.says: The Tribunal may consider Commission policies, and must consider one if a party or intervenor asks it to.

source.expect: the Tribunal shall consider a policy approved by the Commission

items.title: The decision
items.says: A final decision must have written reasons. The Tribunal sends each party a copy; a copy sent by email is deemed received the next day, and by mail on the fifth day after mailing.

source.expect: may not be finally disposed of without written reasons

items.title: Written reasons required
items.says: An application may not be finally disposed of without written reasons.

source.expect: may not be finally disposed of without written reasons

items.title: When a decision is deemed received
items.says: A decision sent by regular mail is deemed received on the fifth day after mailing; one sent electronically is deemed received the next day (or the next non-holiday).

source.expect: deemed to be received by the party on the fifth day

items.title: Referral to the Commission
items.says: The Tribunal may refer matters arising in a proceeding to the Commission if they are of public interest; the Commission decides whether to act.

source.expect: they are matters of public interest

items.title: Order to pay compensation
items.says: If the Tribunal finds a party infringed another party's Code right, it may order payment of compensation for loss arising from the infringement, including compensation for injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect. There is no cap on the amount in the Code.

source.expect: including compensation for injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect

items.title: Order of restitution other than money
items.says: The Tribunal may order the party who infringed a right to make restitution other than money (for example, reinstatement to a job or offering housing) for loss arising out of the infringement.

source.expect: make restitution to the party whose right was infringed, other than through monetary compensation

items.title: Order to promote compliance (public interest remedy)
items.says: The Tribunal may order any party to do anything it thinks that party ought to do to promote compliance with the Code, including about future practices (such as training or policy changes), even if no one asked for it.

source.expect: may direct a person to do anything with respect to future practices

items.title: Orders on a Commission application
items.says: On a Commission application, the Tribunal may order any party to do anything to promote compliance with the Code, including about future practices.

source.expect: to do anything that, in the opinion of the Tribunal

items.title: Interest on money orders
items.says: A tribunal order for payment of money must state the principal amount and, if interest is payable, the rate and the date it runs from.

source.expect: the rate of interest and the date from which it is to be calculated

items.title: Settlement
items.says: A settlement that is in writing and signed by the parties is binding on them. On the parties' joint motion, the Tribunal may make an order requiring compliance with it.

source.expect: agreed to in writing and signed by the parties, the settlement is binding

items.title: Consent order on a settlement
items.says: On the joint motion of the parties, the Tribunal may make an order requiring compliance with all or part of a signed written settlement.

source.expect: on the joint motion of the parties, make an order requiring compliance

items.title: Decision without a hearing on consent
items.says: If the parties consent, a proceeding may be decided without a hearing, unless another law says otherwise.

source.expect: If the parties consent, a proceeding may be disposed of

items.title: Withdrawing an application
items.says: An applicant may withdraw an application by notifying the Tribunal under its rules.

source.citation: Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario Rules of Procedure (amended effective August 17, 2026)
source.expect: withdraw

items.title: Application for contravention of settlement
items.says: If a party believes another party broke a signed written settlement, they may apply to the Tribunal within six months after the breach (or the last breach in a series).

source.expect: within six months after the contravention

items.title: Late contravention applications
items.says: The Tribunal may accept a late contravention application if the delay was in good faith and no one affected will suffer substantial prejudice.

source.expect: the delay was incurred in good faith

items.title: Contravention of settlement form
items.says: A contravention-of-settlement application must be on the Tribunal's approved form. The parties are the parties to the settlement and anyone the Tribunal adds.

source.expect: shall be in a form approved by the Tribunal

items.title: Order remedying a broken settlement
items.says: If the Tribunal finds a party broke the settlement, it may make any order it considers appropriate to remedy the breach.

source.expect: any order that it considers appropriate to remedy the contravention

items.title: Request for reconsideration
items.says: Any party may ask the Tribunal to reconsider its decision under the Tribunal rules, and the Tribunal may also reconsider on its own. Reconsideration is discretionary and is not a second hearing.

source.expect: may request that the Tribunal reconsider its decision

items.title: Time to request reconsideration
items.says: Under the HRTO Rules, a request for reconsideration is filed within 30 days of the decision, unless the Tribunal allows more time in exceptional circumstances.

source.citation: Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario Rules of Procedure (amended effective August 17, 2026)
source.expect: within 30 days of the date of the decision

items.title: Correcting a typo or calculation error
items.says: The Tribunal may at any time correct a typographical error, calculation error or similar error in its decision.

source.expect: correct a typographical error, error of calculation

items.title: Tribunal decisions are final
items.says: A Tribunal decision is final and cannot be appealed. A court on judicial review cannot set it aside unless it is patently unreasonable (subject to reconsideration and correction of errors).

source.expect: unless the decision is patently unreasonable

items.title: Judicial review in the Divisional Court
items.says: A party may apply to the Divisional Court for judicial review of a Tribunal decision. It is started by a notice of application (Form 68A) and is a review of the decision, not a new hearing.

source.expect: the notice of application shall be in Form 68A

items.title: Time limit for judicial review
items.says: An application for judicial review must be made no later than 30 days after the decision, unless the court extends the time.

source.citation: Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
source.expect: no later than 30 days after the date the decision

items.title: Application record and factum
items.says: The applicant on judicial review delivers an application record and a factum within 30 days after the Tribunal's record is filed (or after the application starts, if no record is needed).

source.expect: within thirty days after the record is filed

items.title: Dismissal of a judicial review for delay
items.says: If the applicant does not deliver the record and factum on time, the respondent may move to the registrar to have the application dismissed for delay.

source.expect: to have the application dismissed for delay

items.title: Judicial review does not stop the order automatically
items.says: Applying for judicial review is not an appeal, so it does not automatically stay (pause) the Tribunal's order.

source.expect: is not an appeal within the meaning of subsection (1)

items.title: Standard of review on judicial review
items.says: The Code says a Tribunal decision can be set aside only if patently unreasonable. The Supreme Court's framework for standard of review is in Vavilov; how it applies to the Code's patently unreasonable clause has been addressed by Ontario courts.

source.expect: shall not be altered or set aside in an application for judicial review

items.title: Breaking the Tribunal's own rules is not enough on its own
items.says: A failure by the Tribunal to follow its rules, or how it used its discretion under them, is not a ground to set aside its decision unless it caused a substantial wrong that affected the final result.

source.expect: caused a substantial wrong which affected the final disposition

items.title: Stated case by the Commission
items.says: Where the Commission was a party or intervenor and believes a final decision is inconsistent with a Commission policy, it may ask the Tribunal to state a case on a question of law to the Divisional Court.

source.expect: state a case to the Divisional Court

items.title: Reconsideration after a stated case
items.says: Within 30 days of receiving the Divisional Court's decision on a stated case, any party may ask the Tribunal to reconsider its original decision.

source.expect: Within 30 days of receipt of the decision of the Divisional Court

items.title: Filing a Tribunal order in the Superior Court
items.says: A certified copy of a Tribunal decision or order may be filed in the Superior Court of Justice by a party. Once filed, it is treated as an order of that court and can be enforced like one.

source.expect: may be filed in the Superior Court of Justice by the tribunal or by a party

items.title: Tell the Tribunal within 10 days of filing
items.says: A party who files a Tribunal order in court must notify the Tribunal within 10 days after filing.

source.expect: shall notify the tribunal within 10 days after the filing

items.title: Sheriff enforces money orders
items.says: On receiving a certified copy of a Tribunal order to pay money, the sheriff enforces it as if it were an execution issued by the Superior Court.

source.expect: the sheriff shall enforce the order as if it were an execution

items.title: Writ of seizure and sale
items.says: A creditor under a court order (including a filed Tribunal order) can have a writ of seizure and sale issued, which lets the sheriff seize and sell the debtor's property.

source.expect: the creditor is entitled to the issue of one or more writs of seizure and sale

items.title: Garnishment
items.says: A creditor under an order to pay money can enforce it by garnishing money owed to the debtor by others, such as wages or bank accounts.

source.expect: may enforce it by garnishment of debts payable to the debtor

items.title: Breaking a Tribunal order is an offence
items.says: Contravening s. 9 of the Code or a Tribunal order is an offence with a fine of up to $25,000. A prosecution needs the Attorney General's written consent.

source.expect: liable to a fine of not more than $25,000

items.title: Attorney General's consent to prosecute
items.says: No prosecution for an offence under the Code can be started without the written consent of the Attorney General.

source.expect: except with the consent in writing of the Attorney General

items.title: Code remedies in a civil lawsuit
items.says: In a civil court case, if the court finds a party infringed another party's Code right, it may order compensation (including for injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect) and restitution.

source.expect: in a civil proceeding in a court, the court finds

items.title: No lawsuit based only on the Code
items.says: A person cannot start a court action based only on an infringement of a Code right. The Code claim must be attached to another cause of action, such as wrongful dismissal or breach of contract.

source.expect: does not permit a person to commence an action based solely

items.title: Limitation period for a civil action
items.says: A court action (including one that asks for Code remedies alongside another claim) generally must be started within two years after the claim was discovered.

source.expect: after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered

items.title: Commission public-interest inquiries
items.says: The Commission may conduct an inquiry to carry out its functions if it believes it is in the public interest.

source.expect: if the Commission believes it is in the public interest to do so

items.title: Commission policies
items.says: The Commission may approve policies giving guidance on applying Parts I and II of the Code (for example, on disability accommodation or harassment).

source.expect: to provide guidance in the application of Parts I and II

items.title: Moore v. British Columbia (Education)
items.says: The Supreme Court set out the three-part test for showing discrimination on its face: a protected characteristic, an adverse impact, and the characteristic being a factor in the impact.

source.decision: Moore v. British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61
source.expect: complainants are required to show that they have a characteristic protected

items.title: Meiorin (BCGSEU)
items.says: The Supreme Court set a single test for a workplace standard: adopted for a purpose rationally connected to the job, adopted in good faith, and reasonably necessary, meaning the employer cannot accommodate without undue hardship.

source.decision: British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 3
source.expect: reasonably necessary to the accomplishment of that legitimate work-related purpose

items.title: Grismer
items.says: The Supreme Court applied the Meiorin test to services, not only employment (a driver's licence standard).

source.decision: British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles) v. British Columbia (Council of Human Rights), [1999] 3 S.C.R. 868

items.title: Stewart v. Elk Valley Coal
items.says: The Supreme Court confirmed the three-part Moore test and that the protected ground must be a factor in the adverse treatment; it also addressed addiction and workplace drug policies.

source.decision: Stewart v. Elk Valley Coal Corp., 2017 SCC 30

items.title: O'Malley (Simpsons-Sears)
items.says: The Supreme Court held that intent is not required and that rules neutral on their face can discriminate by their effect (adverse effect discrimination).

source.decision: Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd., [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536

items.title: Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud
items.says: The Supreme Court held that a union can share the duty to accommodate and that the employee seeking accommodation must help find a reasonable accommodation.

source.decision: Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970

items.title: Hydro-Québec v. Syndicat
items.says: The Supreme Court held that undue hardship does not require proof that accommodation is impossible; the test is whether the employer cannot accommodate without undue hardship, for example where the employee cannot work in the reasonably foreseeable future.

source.decision: Hydro-Québec v. Syndicat des employé-e-s de techniques professionnelles et de bureau d'Hydro-Québec, section locale 2000 (SCFP-FTQ), 2008 SCC 43

items.title: Quebec (CDPDJ) v. Bombardier
items.says: The Supreme Court held that each element of discrimination is proved on a balance of probabilities and that the ground need only be a factor, which can be shown by circumstantial evidence.

source.decision: Quebec (Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse) v. Bombardier Inc. (Bombardier Aerospace Training Center), 2015 SCC 39

items.title: Peel Law Association v. Pieters
items.says: The Court of Appeal for Ontario confirmed that a protected ground need only be one factor in the treatment and that discrimination can be inferred from circumstantial evidence.

source.decision: Peel Law Association v. Pieters, 2013 ONCA 396

items.title: Janzen v. Platy Enterprises
items.says: The Supreme Court held that sexual harassment in the workplace is a form of sex discrimination.

source.decision: Janzen v. Platy Enterprises Ltd., [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1252

items.title: Noble v. York University (reprisal test)
items.says: An HRTO decision often cited for the elements of reprisal: an action or threat, an intent (at least in part) to retaliate, and a link to a claim or enforcement of Code rights.

source.decision: Noble v. York University, 2010 HRTO 878

items.title: Seneca College v. Bhadauria
items.says: The Supreme Court held there is no independent tort (civil wrong) of discrimination; the Code's own procedures are the route for Code-only claims.

source.decision: Seneca College of Applied Arts and Technology v. Bhadauria, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 181

items.title: British Columbia (WCB) v. Figliola
items.says: The Supreme Court discussed when a human rights tribunal should not re-decide a matter already decided by another body that had power to decide it, applying principles behind s. 45.1-type provisions.

source.decision: British Columbia (Workers' Compensation Board) v. Figliola, 2011 SCC 52

items.title: Penner v. Niagara (Regional Police Services Board)
items.says: The Supreme Court addressed when a decision in one proceeding prevents re-litigation of the same issue in another (issue estoppel), including fairness of applying it.

source.decision: Penner v. Niagara (Regional Police Services Board), 2013 SCC 19

items.title: Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies
items.says: The Supreme Court set out the test for issue estoppel and the discretion not to apply it where that would be unfair.

source.decision: Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies Inc., 2001 SCC 44

items.title: Tranchemontagne v. Ontario
items.says: The Supreme Court held that an Ontario tribunal with power to decide questions of law can apply the Human Rights Code and decline to apply a provision that conflicts with it.

source.decision: Tranchemontagne v. Ontario (Director, Disability Support Program), 2006 SCC 14

items.title: Northern Regional Health Authority v. Horrocks
items.says: The Supreme Court addressed whether a labour arbitrator or a human rights tribunal has jurisdiction over workplace human rights disputes in a unionized setting, depending on the statutes in each province.

source.decision: Northern Regional Health Authority v. Horrocks, 2021 SCC 42

items.title: Canada (MCI) v. Vavilov
items.says: The Supreme Court set the framework for the standard of review of administrative decisions, including that courts give effect to a legislature's choice of a standard.

source.decision: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65

items.title: Arunachalam v. Best Buy Canada
items.says: An HRTO decision often cited for the factors used to set compensation for injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect: the objective seriousness of the conduct and its effect on the particular applicant.

source.decision: Arunachalam v. Best Buy Canada, 2010 HRTO 1880

items.title: ADGA Group Consultants v. Lane
items.says: The Divisional Court upheld an HRTO award for a disability-related dismissal, including damages for injury to dignity and the failure to take part in the procedural duty to accommodate.

source.decision: ADGA Group Consultants Inc. v. Lane (2008), 91 O.R. (3d) 649 (Div. Ct.)

items.title: Taylor-Baptiste v. OPSEU
items.says: The Court of Appeal for Ontario upheld the HRTO's approach to whether conduct falls within a social area ('with respect to employment') and its balancing of Code rights with freedom of expression.

source.decision: Taylor-Baptiste v. Ontario Public Service Employees Union, 2015 ONCA 495

items.title: Shaw v. Phipps
items.says: The Court of Appeal for Ontario upheld an HRTO finding of racial profiling based on circumstantial evidence.

source.decision: Shaw v. Phipps, 2012 ONCA 155
